extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigators, judges, and scholars handling Korean patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural/substantive criteria for administrative revocation suits (IPTAB-related) and civil patent infringement litigation in Korea, including claim construction, infringement analyses, defenses, evidence, and remedies. Focused on what courts and parties must plead, prove, and how courts examine issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of administrative patent litigation & IPTAB prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative litigation concerning patents is divided into categories; certain categories (e.g., appeals against IPTAB decisions) always require the IPTAB’s decision before lodging a lawsuit with the Patent Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative litigation that falls under the first category always requires the IPTAB’s decision before filing with the Patent Court; other categories may be instituted without the adjudication process. (Citation: Patent Act, art. 186(6); Administrative Litigation Act, art. 18(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable laws for revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Revocation suits (litigation for the revocation of IPTAB decisions) are administrative litigation governed primarily by the Patent Act, with the Administrative Litigation Act applied mutatis mutandis and the Civil Procedure Act filling gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because revocation suits are administrative in nature, matters not in the Patent Act follow the Administrative Litigation Act and, where unspecified there, the Civil Procedure Act. Litigation and evidence procedures follow these statutes (see Section 8.6 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of revocation suits (original disposition principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A revocation suit can generally only be filed against the original disposition (principle of original dispositions), except where the adjudication itself is legally flawed (exceptional adjudication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suits against adjudications are allowed only as prescribed by the Patent Act; you cannot sue claiming 'patent X shall become null and void' — the complaint must seek revocation of the IPTAB decision (specifying date and case number).

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigant standing in revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a party to the IPTAB trial, an intervenor, or a person denied intervention has standing to institute a revocation suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In ex parte revocation suits (e.g., examiner rejection), the Commissioner of KIPO is defendant. In inter partes revocation suits, petitioners/respondents in the IPTAB proceeding are defendants; the party who received an unfavorable IPTAB ruling typically becomes the plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing period for revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A revocation suit must be filed within 30 days from service of a certified copy of the IPTAB decision or ruling; suits filed after this are dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 30-day period is not extendable/shortenable by the court. The IPTAB presiding judge may ex officio grant additional time (e.g., for remote or foreign parties), but an extension granted after the initial 30 days has lapsed does not cure a late suit. (Patent Act, arts. 186(3)-(6)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of examination in revocation suits (limitation vs nonlimitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revocation suits examine the unlawfulness of the administrative disposition (substantive and procedural). There is debate whether examination is limited to grounds raised at IPTAB (limitation theory) or can consider new reasons (nonlimitation theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inter partes cases, the Supreme Court supports the nonlimitation theory: courts may examine and judge reasons not ruled on by IPTAB unless special circumstances advise otherwise. For ex parte cases, the Commissioner cannot raise new grounds of rejection that were not raised before the examiner/IPTAB because the applicant lacked opportunity to respond; this protection is aimed at procedural rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaint contents for revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The complaint must detail the IPTAB procedural background, a summary of the administrative decision (arguments and IPTAB's ruling), parts admitted/not admitted among grounds, all arguments for revocation, related cases, and the plaintiff’s plan to request evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required attachments include power of attorney, corporate registration or nationality certificate (for foreign corporations), certificate of service of the administrative decision, and evidentiary documents specific to the type of revocation (e.g., IPTAB decision, patent application, examiner's rejections and amendments for rejection cases; original register and prior art evidence for invalidation cases). Notification to IPTAB President is required when a revocation suit is lodged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer contents for revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant must submit an answer within three weeks from service of the complaint containing: answer to demand, admitted/not-admitted parts of plaintiff’s arguments, detailed rebuttals, other arguments to maintain the decision, related cases, acceptance/denial of plaintiff’s evidentiary documents, and the defendant's plan to request evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answers should be accompanied by supporting evidence and explanatory documents for any evidence cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparatory hearing topics in revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A preparatory hearing addresses scheduling and procedural management issues prior to trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common matters: dates/number of trials and issues per trial; deadlines for submissions (briefs, expert affidavits, number/length of briefs); whether time-consuming evidentiary methods (verification, appraisal, expert witness) are needed and deadlines for them; designation of technical advisor; technical explanatory sessions; whether to hold claim construction hearing first; pending correction petitions handling; possibility of parallel hearings with related cases; confirmation/summary of disputed issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal technical explanatory session
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the hearing date, the court holds an internal technical explanatory session to improve understanding of technical issues, usually led by a technical examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sessions cover technology background, technical issues relating to the invention and prior art. Unlike civil patent cases (where omitted if no technical issue), these sessions are held in almost all revocation suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing conduct in revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings involve evidence examination linked to party arguments, identification and sharing of key issues, oral argument on key issues, and applications for further evidence; revocation suits typically receive more time due to technical matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revocation suits focus on technical issues like inventive step and often close after an intensive first round of examination. First hearing may be arranged as a technical explanatory session. Parties can present arguments in a foreign language with consent and court permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship and parallel examination with infringement proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Related cases involving the same IP registration number are generally allocated to the same judicial panel; when infringement and revocation cases involving the same patent and parties are before the same panel and parallel hearing is needed, the court will normally hold trials in parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must notify panels when related cases are pending before different panels to allow reallocation and avoid inconsistent adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence collection procedures in revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence types and request processes are similar to civil litigation, but the court may examine evidence ex officio if necessary; nonetheless, the principle of pleadings governs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court's ex officio examination is supplementary and limited to evidence on record — not a broad doctrine of the court discovering facts independently. (Administrative Litigation Act, art. 26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from revocation suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of the Patent Court in revocation cases may be appealed to the Supreme Court, following appeal procedures similar to civil cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Section 8.8 and Patent Act art. 186(8) for procedural details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a court decision revoking an IPTAB decision
rubrics_metrics.description: When a court revokes an IPTAB decision and the revocation becomes final, the IPTAB decision becomes void and IPTAB must reconsider and render another decision; the revocation grounds are binding on IPTAB for that case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example workflow: examiner rejection → IPTAB dismissal → Patent Court revokes IPTAB → Supreme Court affirms → IPTAB revokes rejection and grants appeal → examiner grants patent. (Patent Act, art. 189(2)-(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of patent infringement and license effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement occurs when a non-patentee/non-exclusive-licensee practices a patented invention for business purposes without permission. Exclusive licenses grant monopoly and can be exercised to seek damages/injunctions (subject to registration); nonexclusive licenses lack monopoly and generally cannot seek damages/injunctions independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration is required for an exclusive license to take effect; nonexclusive licenses need registration to be effective against third parties. Where an exclusive license covers the entire patent, the patentee may still seek injunctions (but not damages without joining the exclusive licensee). (Patent Act arts. 94,100–102,118–101).

rubrics_metrics.name: Available remedies for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Once infringement is established, the patentee may seek damages (Article 750 Civil Act; Article 128(1) Patent Act), restitution of unjust enrichment, preliminary or permanent injunctions (Article 126 Patent Act), recovery of reputation, and possibly criminal liability (Article 225 Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of remedy depends on case facts; damages and injunctions have different procedural and substantive requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements required to establish infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must prove ownership of the patent and that the defendant has 'practiced' the patent; defendant's product or method must fall within the scope of protection of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice for business purposes includes manufacturing, using, assigning, leasing, importing, offering to assign/lease (including display), using/offering to use a process, or being about to commit such acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction as legal determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of protection is determined by the claims and claim construction is a legal evaluation (not fact-finding) to be performed before assessing infringement, novelty, or inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction should determine the objective scope the patent effects reach; it cannot be established by confession and must be based primarily on claim wording with reference to descriptions/drawings and technical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are construed mainly by the literal wording (principle of literal interpretation), but descriptions/drawings (reference to description) and general technical knowledge at filing are used to ascertain technical meaning. Prosecution history may be referenced but must not be used to broaden or narrow claim wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to applicant's arguments, amendments, written arguments, and examiner opinions is permitted for accurate understanding but cannot alter the claim's meaning beyond its wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement analysis and all-elements rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement analysis breaks the disputed claim into elements and compares each element (and their organic combination) to the defendant’s product or process; all elements as confirmed by claim construction must be present for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties often prepare one-to-one comparison charts. If any element is missing, the defendant’s product/process falls outside the protected scope (all elements rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Literal infringement is established when all claim elements and their specified combination are found in the defendant’s product/process under literal interpretation of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic type of infringement claim; courts apply the literal meaning determined in claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by equivalence (positive and negative requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalence is found when defendant’s elements are not literally identical but are equivalent to claim elements, subject to positive requirements (shared problem-solving principle; substantially identical effects; replacement is obvious to person skilled in art) and negative requirements (defendant's technology not free-to-practice/public domain; replaced element not intentionally excluded during prosecution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof: patentee proves positive requirements; infringer proves negative requirements. Determination requires substantive review of the underlying technical idea (essence of technical solution) with reference to detailed description and prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain acts (manufacturing, assigning, leasing, importing, offering to assign/lease items exclusively used for making/practicing a patented product/process) done for business purposes constitute indirect infringement under Article 127.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must prove three elements: (i) the alleged good is used in practicing the patented invention (use requirement); (ii) the good is exclusively used in practicing the patented invention (exclusivity requirement); and (iii) the good is made for business purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive categories and defendant disclosure obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses are legally cognizable rebuttals (burden on defendant); denials challenge plaintiff’s proof (burden on plaintiff). A defendant denying infringement must disclose the product/process actually used; refusal without justification may lead the court to presume infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under amended Patent Act provisions, courts may draw adverse inferences if a defendant refuses to provide details of the product/process used. Denial examples include arguing the patent right doesn't exist or the defendant's technology does not fall within the claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of rights defense (review of inventive step in infringement suits)
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is clear that the patented invention lacks an inventive step (or is invalid for novelty/description), claims for damages or injunctions may constitute an abuse of rights; courts handling infringement suits may review inventive step to assess this defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court permits the infringement court to decide inventive step when the defense is raised. The plaintiff may respond with a correction/reply to narrow or correct claims, provided the correction does not substantially alter the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-to-exploit technology defense
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant's product consists only of publicly known technologies or can be easily practiced from public knowledge, the defendant need not be compared element-by-element to conclude the exploited technology is outside the patent scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defense resembles inventive step analysis but compares the defendant's product to known technologies (not the patented invention). It is rarely used because abuse-of-rights is often invoked instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known technology defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may assert that the patented invention was publicly known or in public use at filing time, bearing the burden of contention and proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defense can be asserted alongside free-to-exploit arguments but is less frequently used in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent exhaustion (first sale) doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Resale or use of a lawfully transferred patented product is generally permitted and does not constitute infringement — the exhaustion doctrine applies to product inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not expressly in the Patent Act, the Supreme Court has acknowledged the doctrine for product inventions; defendants may raise patent exhaustion as a defense in infringement suits.
